summary: Year 2 (age 6–7) money problems stay within a single unit (pence): totalling the cost of items, and the more demanding work of finding change and answering 'how much more do I need?'. The core idea is that change is a DIFFERENCE, most easily reached by COUNTING UP from the price to the amount paid (the 'shopkeeper's method') with real coins, rather than by counting back or written take-away. Change should be a practical, coin-in-hand act before it becomes an abstract subtraction.
misconceptions: 'More coins = more money' — thinks a fistful of small coins is worth more, so gives too many or judges having-enough by count not value.
Adds the two numbers (price + amount paid) instead of finding the difference, because early teaching over-emphasises 'take away' and difference is not recognised as subtraction.
Loses the running total or miscounts when bridging through a multiple of ten while counting up.
Counts single pennies one-by-one inaccurately instead of using coin values.

activities.title: Give change at a role-play market stall (count up with coins)
steps: Set up a shop: a toy priced 35p, a 50p coin to pay with, and a pot of mixed coins.
Count UP aloud from the price to the amount paid, placing a coin into a change tray at each step: '35… (put in a 5p) 40… (put in a 10p) 50'.
State the change as the coins you built: 'The change is 15p — a 10p and a 5p.'
Check by counting the change back onto the price to confirm it rebuilds the amount paid (35p + 15p = 50p).
Repeat with other friendly prices (e.g. 45p paid with 50p gives 5p), then extend to the source worked example 27p paid with 50p, counting 27→30→50 to give 3p + 20p = 23p.
activities.insight: Change is the DISTANCE travelled from the price up to the amount paid — it is the total of the jumps you make when counting up (here 5p + 10p = 15p), not a take-away you have to work out on paper. The coins themselves record how the change was reached.

activities.title: 'How much more do I need?' — the same gap read the other way
steps: Set a toy priced 20p and give the child 15p.
Ask: 'How much MORE do you need to buy this?'
Count UP from what you have to the price: '15… (add a 5p) 20' and name the shortfall as 5p.
Line this up against a change task: notice that finding the shortfall and finding change are the same counting-up move, just started from a different amount.
activities.insight: Finding change and finding 'how much more I need' (missing addend) are one idea: closing the gap by counting up between two amounts.

activities.title: Value, not number of coins
steps: Lay the child's handful of small coins beside a single 10p and 5p.
Count the total VALUE of each set and compare, e.g. show that ten 1p coins are worth less than one 20p.
Make the SAME value (e.g. 15p) with different coin combinations (10p + 5p; 5p + 5p + 5p; 10p + 2p + 2p + 1p).
activities.insight: Money is judged by total value, not by how many coins there are; many small coins can be worth less than one larger coin.

activities.title: Short written check on change and coin combinations
steps: Given a price and an amount paid, state the change and the coins that make it.
Pick, from a set of options, coins that make a given change, and set a value (e.g. with a slider) to match the change for a given purchase.
activities.insight: A quick check confirms whether the child can land the correct change amount and a valid coin combination.

checkQuestion: Set out a toy labelled 35p and give the child a single 50p coin and a pot of mixed coins. Say: 'Buy the toy and give me the right change — use the coins to show me how you work it out.' Then set a second toy at 20p and say: 'You have 15p. How much more do you need to buy this one?' Watch HOW they work, not just the answer.
checkAnswer: For change: counts up from 35p (e.g. +5p to 40p, +10p to 50p) and hands back 15p in coins, or otherwise establishes the 15p gap and gives it by value. For the second: identifies the 5p shortfall by counting on from 15p to 20p. In both, the coins/steps show a DIFFERENCE being built, and the child can check by rebuilding the paid amount.
